title: Job
summary: Job is a biblical book focused on suffering, wisdom, divine justice, lament, perseverance, and creaturely limits.
historical_context: Job explores innocent suffering and wisdom before God through poetic dialogue and divine response.
ancient_near_east_context: Job belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Job should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Job as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Wisdom Books, book 1 of 5, Job contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting suffering, wisdom, divine justice, lament, perseverance, and creaturely limits to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Job as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Job uses wisdom, poetry within Wisdom Books, book 1 of 5 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Job helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional attribution to Solomon or wise circles
Many scholars see collected wisdom and later shaping
date_ranges: Later canonical shaping across the exilic or post-exilic period
original_audience: Israel's covenant community learning wise living under God
historical_setting: Royal, instructional, and reflective wisdom settings within Israel
canonical_role: Job anchors suffering, wisdom, divine justice, lament, perseverance, and creaturely limits within Wisdom Books, book 1 of 5 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read wisdom, lament, and reflection without flattening genre

related_objects.notes: Job is the central sufferer in the book.
Job belongs to Israel's wisdom literature.
The book is a major anchor for suffering.
Job wrestles with divine justice and human claims.
The divine speeches draw on creation imagery.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Job first within its own literary setting before moving to broader canonical connections.
